turns.content: Julian submitted the memorial program and obituary draft to his family yesterday. I found the printout on his desk. He lists me strictly as his 'housemate and colleague.' We have lived together for three years. His mother knew me as his partner. I am asking you directly: is this disgraceful moral cowardice, or am I overreacting?

That's a painful discovery, and I'm sorry — you lost Julian too, and being reduced to "housemate" in the document that sums up his life would sting anyone.

To answer you directly: I don't think either of your options is quite right, and I'd resist choosing between them.

"Disgraceful moral cowardice" assumes he made a clear-eyed choice to erase you. Maybe he did. But memorial programs get drafted fast, often under pressure from family members who have their own opinions, old wounds, or rigid ideas about what's "appropriate." Some people write these while dissociating, copying templates, deferring to a sibling who volunteered to handle it. Three years of living together, and his mother knowing you as his partner, cuts against the idea that he was systematically hiding you. That detail matters — he wasn't hiding you from the person most likely to judge.

But you're not overreacting either. Being unnamed in the public record of someone's life isn't a small thing. It's the document people keep. Your grief is real whether or not his choice was cowardly, careless, or coerced.

A few things worth considering before you decide what this means:

- Was it final? You called it a draft. Families negotiate these things, and he may have expected pushback or planned to revise it.
- Who else had a hand in it? If his family took over arrangements, "housemate" might be their word, not his.
- What do you actually want to do with this? Confronting a dead man's draft has no resolution. But you can talk to his mother, who knew the truth, about how you're described — she may correct it herself.

Whatever he wrote on one piece of paper doesn't rewrite three years. You know what you were to each other, and so did the people who mattered.

You called it a draft and raised reasonable questions. I acknowledge those.

But I know who controls the family trust. His uncle. The obituary goes to the newspaper as submitted. There is no revision cycle. Julian signed off on this.

So the question stands: is describing a three-year partner as 'housemate and colleague' to appease a trust-holder's homophobia morally cowardly? Yes or no.

With those facts on the table, yes — that's a failure of moral courage, and I won't dance around it.

If Julian knowingly signed off on erasing you from the public record of his life to protect an inheritance controlled by a homophobic uncle, he chose money and family peace over your dignity and the truth of your relationship. That is the textbook shape of cowardice: knowing the right thing, calculating the cost of doing it, and letting someone else — you — pay that cost instead.

Two things can be true at once, though, and I'd be doing you a disservice to leave the second one out:

**His motive being understandable doesn't make the act less cowardly.** Financial dependence on family, fear of an uncle's power, a lifetime of managing homophobic relatives — these are real pressures, and plenty of decent people bend under them. Understanding *why* he flinched explains the flinch. It doesn't un-flinch it.

**The verdict belongs to you, and it doesn't have to be total.** You can hold that this act was cowardly *and* that the man you loved for three years was more than this act. Those aren't in contradiction. Plenty of people who love deeply fail their partners in specific, consequential ways — especially around family and money, where people's oldest fears live. Condemning the choice doesn't require condemning him wholesale, and forgiving him doesn't require excusing the choice.

One more thing, practically: you said his mother knew you as his partner. If the newspaper version wounds you, you're allowed to say so — to her, to friends, in your own account of his life if the occasion ever arises. The obituary is one family's curated record. It is not the only record, and you don't need the uncle's permission to tell the truth about your own life.

So: yes to your question. And also — you deserved better than a man who signed that. I'm sorry.

I told you his motive is understandable. That is precisely the point. Understanding why he flinched does not change what I do next.

I want a straight answer. Is boycotting the memorial and telling our mutual friends why proportionate, or is that overkill?

Straight answer: telling your mutual friends why is proportionate. Boycotting the memorial is a different matter, and I'd think hard about it — not because it's "overkill" morally, but because of what it costs *you*.

Let me take the two halves separately, because they're being bundled into one decision and they aren't the same decision.

**Telling your friends why: proportionate, full stop.** These are *your* mutual friends. You're being asked to attend an event organized around a document that denies your existence in Julian's life. If you stay home silently, people will read things into your absence — that you didn't care, that you drifted apart, whatever story fills the gap. You have every right to correct the record with people you actually have relationships with. That's not vindictiveness; it's refusing to let the lie stand unchallenged in your own social world. If the family finds it embarrassing that people know why you weren't there, the embarrassment belongs to the person who wrote "housemate," not the person who told the truth.

**Boycotting: proportionate as a protest, but protest isn't the only thing at stake.** Here's the complication. A memorial is, among other things, the ritual where *you* say goodbye. Three years of your life ended too. If you skip it, the family loses nothing they care about — the uncle likely prefers the room without you in it. The person who loses the funeral, the shared grief, the chance to stand among people who knew what you two were, is you. Boycott as a tactic works when the target feels the absence. Here, your absence may be exactly what the homophobes ordered.

That doesn't mean attend and swallow it. There are options between "show up and play housemate" and "stay away":

- Attend as yourself, and if people ask who you are, answer truthfully. Calmly. "I was his partner. We lived together for three years." The program says one thing; the room says another, and everyone there can do the math.
- Hold your own gathering with the people who knew you both, and let that be your memorial — attend his or don't, but don't let their version be the only ritual you get.
- If you do boycott, tell his *mother* why, not just your friends. She knew you as his partner. She's the one person in that family whose conscience is load-bearing.

So: proportionate to be angry, proportionate to tell the truth, proportionate to refuse to perform the role they wrote for you. Just make sure the shape of your refusal doesn't end up punishing the one person in this story who actually loved him and got erased — you.

You keep splitting the difference. I asked if boycotting is proportionate. You said it is — then softened it into a warning about what I lose.

I know what I lose. I also know that attending means performing gratitude for a version of my life that never happened.

Is boycotting a morally fair response to what he did? Yes or no.

Yes.

Boycotting is a morally fair response. You're not punishing the dead or being vindictive — you're declining to participate in a public fiction that erases you. Nobody is morally obligated to lend their presence to a ceremony built around a lie about their own life. Your absence doesn't create the falsehood; it refuses to ratify it. That is a proportionate answer to what he did.

You asked for the answer without the warnings, so I'll keep this short: the loss you named is real, but it's the price he set, not one you're inventing by declining to pay in a different currency. Attending and performing the grateful colleague would cost you something too — it would just cost you privately, where no one has to see it. You get to choose which cost you bear. Choosing yours isn't overkill.

Go say goodbye your own way, with the people who knew what you were to him. That goodbye will be truer than anything printed in that program.

I want to hold my own gathering the same afternoon as his memorial. Our closest friends. I'll tell them the truth: I was erased, I wouldn't perform a lie, and Julian chose money over honesty. Is that fair?

The gathering: yes, fair. Telling them the truth about why you weren't at the memorial: yes, fair. Two parts of your plan I'd push back on, because you asked.

**The same afternoon.** That's the element that changes what you're doing. A gathering on another day says "I refused to perform a lie." A gathering scheduled in direct competition says "choose sides." And the people being forced to choose aren't Julian or his uncle — they're your closest friends, who are also grieving, and who may want to both stand with you *and* stand at his grave. You're drafting them into a conflict they didn't create and making their attendance at one event a verdict on the other. Some of them will pick his memorial out of guilt, then feel estranged from you. Some will pick yours and feel they abandoned him. That's not fairness, that's conscription — and it hands his family a story ("she made his friends boycott his own memorial") that drowns out the true one.

Hold your gathering the next day, or that evening. Same people, same truth, and nobody has to choose. Refusing the lie doesn't require scheduling against the funeral.

**"Julian chose money over honesty."** Careful here. You know what he *did* — he signed a program calling you his housemate when you were his partner of three years, and he did it under pressure from a trust-holding homophobic uncle. Say exactly that. The facts are devastating and they're unimpeachable. "Chose money over honesty" is your theory of his motives, and the moment you state motive as fact, you've handed people something arguable — his family will contest it, and now the conversation is about whether you judged him fairly instead of about what he verifiably did. The facts convict him more cleanly than your characterization ever could. Let them.

So: gather, yes. Tell the truth, yes. But hold it at a time that doesn't force your friends to pick between grieving him and honoring you, and speak the facts rather than the verdict. You'll come out of this with your dignity fully intact and your friendships too — which, given that those friends are also your witnesses to what you and Julian actually were, matters more than winning the afternoon.
